claim: Normal aging leads to myelin alterations in the rhesus monkey dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC), which are positively correlated with degree of cognitive impairment.
source: Normal aging leads to myelin alterations in the rhesus monkey dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC), which are positively correlated with degree of cognitive impairment.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies showing myelin alterations and their correlation with cognitive impairment in aging monkeys.

claim: Remyelination with shorter and thinner myelin sheaths partially compensates for myelin degradation.
source: It is hypothesized that remyelination with shorter and thinner myelin sheaths partially compensates for myelin degradation, but computational modeling has not yet explored these two phenomena together systematically.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis that has not been systematically explored computationally.

claim: Biologically plausible levels of myelin dystrophy, if uncompensated by other factors, can account for substantial working memory impairment with aging.
source: While complete remyelination nearly recovered axonal transmission and network function to unperturbed levels, our models predict that biologically plausible levels of myelin dystrophy, if uncompensated by other factors, can account for substantial working memory impairment with aging.
evidence: This is a prediction from the computational models presented in the study.

claim: Normal aging often leads to impairment in some cognitive domains in humans.
source: Normal aging often leads to impairment in some cognitive domains, as evidenced by reduced performance on learning and memory tasks in both humans (Albert, 1993; Salthouse et al., 2003; Fisk and Sharp, 2004; Rhodes, 2004; Sorel and Pennequin, 2008) and non-human primates (Moore et al., 2006; Shamy et al., 2011; Moore et al., 2017; Comrie et al., 2018; Chang et al., 2022; Moore et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to empirical studies in humans.

claim: Normal aging often leads to impairment in some cognitive domains in non-human primates.
source: Normal aging often leads to impairment in some cognitive domains, as evidenced by reduced performance on learning and memory tasks in both humans (Albert, 1993; Salthouse et al., 2003; Fisk and Sharp, 2004; Rhodes, 2004; Sorel and Pennequin, 2008) and non-human primates (Moore et al., 2006; Shamy et al., 2011; Moore et al., 2017; Comrie et al., 2018; Chang et al., 2022; Moore et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to empirical studies in non-human primates.

claim: Age-related working memory decline in rhesus monkeys is accompanied by sublethal structural and functional changes in vascular elements, individual pyramidal neurons, glial cells, and white matter pathways.
source: In the rhesus monkey, age-related working memory decline is accompanied by sublethal structural and functional changes in vascular elements, individual pyramidal neurons, glial cells, and white matter pathways (reviews: Hof and Morrison, 2004; Luebke et al., 2010; Peters and Kemper, 2012; Morrison and Baxter, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles summarizing empirical findings.

claim: Cortical neurons do not die during normal aging.
source: It is well documented that cortical neurons do not die during normal aging but rather undergo a number of morphological and physiological alterations, particularly in the monkey dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC), the critical cortical circuit for working memory.
evidence: This is stated as a well-documented fact in the field.

claim: The monkey dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) is the critical cortical circuit for working memory.
source: It is well documented that cortical neurons do not die during normal aging but rather undergo a number of morphological and physiological alterations, particularly in the monkey dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC), the critical cortical circuit for working memory.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: During normal aging, Layer 3 pyramidal neurons in rhesus monkey dlPFC exhibit a significant loss of dendritic spines and synapses.
source: For example, during normal aging Layer 3 pyramidal neurons in rhesus monkey dlPFC exhibit a significant loss of dendritic spines and synapses (Chang et al., 2005; Peters et al., 2008; Chang et al., 2022), and electrophysiological changes observed both in vitro (Chang et al., 2005; Ibañez et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2022) and in vivo during a spatial working memory task (Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Layer 3 pyramidal neurons in rhesus monkey dlPFC exhibit electrophysiological changes during normal aging both in vitro and in vivo during a spatial working memory task.
source: For example, during normal aging Layer 3 pyramidal neurons in rhesus monkey dlPFC exhibit a significant loss of dendritic spines and synapses (Chang et al., 2005; Peters et al., 2008; Chang et al., 2022), and electrophysiological changes observed both in vitro (Chang et al., 2005; Ibañez et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2022) and in vivo during a spatial working memory task (Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Extensive myelin dystrophy during normal aging has been observed in both gray and white matter.
source: Perhaps most strikingly, extensive myelin dystrophy during normal aging has been observed in both gray and white matter (Peters et al., 2001; Bowley et al., 2010; review: Peters, 2007), including in monkey dlPFC (Peters and Sethares, 2002; Peters and Sethares, 2003; review: Peters, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies and reviews.

claim: 3–6% of myelin sheaths in dlPFC exhibit age-related alterations including splitting of the major dense line of the myelin sheath, balloons, and redundant myelin.
source: Ultrastructural studies reveal that 3–6% of myelin sheaths in dlPFC exhibit age-related alterations including splitting of the major dense line of the myelin sheath, balloons, and redundant myelin (Figure 1; Peters and Sethares, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to an empirical study and reference to Figure 1 showing examples of these alterations.

claim: Remyelination has been observed across the adult lifespan in monkey dlPFC.
source: Remyelination has also been observed across the adult lifespan in monkey dlPFC and there is a 90% increase in the number of paranodal profiles in aged versus young monkeys, indicating higher numbers of internodal myelin sheaths with aging (Peters and Sethares, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to an empirical study.

claim: There is a 90% increase in the number of paranodal profiles in aged versus young monkeys.
source: Remyelination has also been observed across the adult lifespan in monkey dlPFC and there is a 90% increase in the number of paranodal profiles in aged versus young monkeys, indicating higher numbers of internodal myelin sheaths with aging (Peters and Sethares, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to an empirical study.

claim: Aged subjects had a significant proportion of abnormally short and thin myelin sheaths.
source: Aged subjects also had a significant proportion of abnormally short and thin myelin sheaths (Peters and Sethares, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to an empirical study.

claim: Myelin degradation begins as oligodendrocytes degenerate due to oxidative stress.
source: The hypothesized mechanism to explain these findings (review:Peters, 2009) is that myelin degradation begins as oligodendrocytes degenerate due to oxidative stress, and that axons accumulate dense inclusions in spaces between the lamellae of their associated myelin sheaths.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesized mechanism from a review article.

claim: As oligodendrocytes die, the associated sheaths detach from the axolemma, leaving bare axonal sections (complete demyelination).
source: As oligodendrocytes die, the associated sheaths detach from the axolemma, leaving bare axonal sections (complete demyelination).
evidence: This is part of the hypothesized mechanism for myelin degradation.

claim: Surviving mature oligodendrocytes remyelinate the bare segments, but with shorter and thinner sheaths.
source: Subsequently, surviving mature oligodendrocytes remyelinate the bare segments, but with shorter and thinner sheaths.
evidence: This is part of the hypothesized mechanism for remyelination after myelin degradation.

claim: The altered sheaths lead to a slowdown of signal propagation that contributes to cognitive slowing/impairment with aging.
source: It is highly plausible that the altered sheaths lead to a slowdown of signal propagation that contributes to cognitive slowing/impairment with aging.
evidence: This is stated as a plausible hypothesis.

claim: Several of the changes that pyramidal neurons undergo with aging correlate with the degree of observed cognitive impairment.
source: Indeed, several of the changes that pyramidal neurons undergo with aging correlate with the degree of observed cognitive impairment (review: Luebke et al., 2010; Peters and Kemper, 2012; Shobin et al., 2017; Moore et al., 2023), including myelin dystrophies and remyelination (Peters and Sethares, 2002; Peters and Sethares, 2003; Dimovasili et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles and empirical studies.

claim: Myelin dystrophies and remyelination correlate with the degree of observed cognitive impairment.
source: Indeed, several of the changes that pyramidal neurons undergo with aging correlate with the degree of observed cognitive impairment (review: Luebke et al., 2010; Peters and Kemper, 2012; Shobin et al., 2017; Moore et al., 2023), including myelin dystrophies and remyelination (Peters and Sethares, 2002; Peters and Sethares, 2003; Dimovasili et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Which changes are the key determinants of age-related cognitive decline has not yet been firmly established.
source: However, which changes are the key determinants of age-related cognitive decline has not yet been firmly established (Konar et al., 2016; Motley et al., 2018; Cleeland et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations indicating ongoing uncertainty in the field.

claim: Computational models become essential to predict how age-related changes in individual neurons affect cognitive impairment.
source: This is in part due to the difficulty of isolating some individual neuronal features (e.g. firing rate, synapses, myelin) empirically, while controlling for concomitant changes in others. Thus, computational models become essential to predict how age-related changes in individual neurons affect cognitive impairment.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the difficulty of empirical isolation of individual features.

claim: Demyelination leads to slower AP CV and sometimes to AP failure.
source: Demyelination has been modeled frequently in the context of disease (review: Coggan et al., 2015), showing that loss of myelin leads to slower AP CV and sometimes to AP failure.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review of modeling studies.

claim: Remyelination of axons with shorter, thinner internodes decreases CV in models of both large- and small-diameter axons.
source: Remyelination of axons with shorter, thinner internodes decreases CV in models of both large- and small-diameter axons (Lasiene et al., 2008; Powers et al., 2012; Scurfield and Latimer, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to modeling studies.

claim: The effects of widespread demyelination and remyelination on AP propagation in a broad population of axons have not been explored systematically.
source: However, to our knowledge, the effects of widespread demyelination and remyelination on AP propagation in a broad population of axons have not been explored systematically.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the literature based on the authors' knowledge.

claim: The empirically observed age-related increase in AP firing rates in prefrontal pyramidal neurons and loss of up to 30% of both excitatory and inhibitory synapses can lead to working memory impairment.
source: Our recent network model revealed that the empirically observed age-related increase in AP firing rates in prefrontal pyramidal neurons (modeled through an increased slope of the f-I curve) and loss of up to 30% of both excitatory and inhibitory synapses (modeled as a decrease in connectivity strength) can lead to working memory impairment (Ibañez et al., 2019), but this model did not incorporate the known changes to myelin structure that occur during normal aging.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous modeling study by the authors.

claim: Higher degrees of demyelination led to slower propagation and eventual failure of APs along the axons of the multicompartment models.
source: Higher degrees of demyelination led to slower propagation and eventual failure of APs along the axons of the multicompartment models.
evidence: This is a finding from the computational models presented in the study.

claim: In the network models, an increase in AP failure rate resulted in progressive working memory impairment.
source: In the network models, an increase in AP failure rate resulted in progressive working memory impairment, whereas slower conduction velocities, in the range observed in the multicompartment models, had a negligible effect.
evidence: This is a finding from the network models presented in the study.

claim: Slower conduction velocities, in the range observed in the multicompartment models, had a negligible effect on working memory in the network models.
source: In the network models, an increase in AP failure rate resulted in progressive working memory impairment, whereas slower conduction velocities, in the range observed in the multicompartment models, had a negligible effect.
evidence: This is a finding from the network models presented in the study.

claim: Sufficient remyelination of all previously demyelinated segments led to a recovery of signal transmission and working memory performance.
source: Sufficient remyelination of all previously demyelinated segments led to a recovery of signal transmission and working memory performance.
evidence: This is a finding from the computational models presented in the study.

claim: Empirically observed levels of myelin changes, if uncompensated by other factors, would lead to substantial working memory impairment with aging.
source: However, our study indicates that empirically observed levels of myelin changes, if uncompensated by other factors, would lead to substantial working memory impairment with aging.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the computational models presented in the study.

claim: Removing 25% of lamellae had a negligible effect on CV, regardless of how many segments were affected.
source: Removing 25% of lamellae had a negligible effect on CV, regardless of how many segments were affected.
evidence: This is a finding from the single neuron model simulations.

claim: When all lamellae were removed, CV slowed drastically – by 38±10% even when just 25% of the segments were demyelinated in this way, and 35±13% of APs failed.
source: However, when all lamellae were removed, CV slowed drastically – by 38±10% even when just 25% of the segments were demyelinated in this way, and 35±13% of APs failed.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the single neuron model simulations.

claim: When 75% of segments lost all their lamellae, CV slowed by 72±8% and 45±13% of APs failed.
source: When 75% of segments lost all their lamellae, CV slowed by 72±8% and 45±13% of APs failed.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the single neuron model simulations.

claim: Myelinated segment length had the largest magnitude with a negative weight indicating that models with longer myelinated segments show more CV slowing in response to a given demyelination perturbation.
source: Among them, myelinated segment length had the largest magnitude with a negative weight indicating that models with longer myelinated segments show more CV slowing in response to a given demyelination perturbation.
evidence: This is a finding from the Lasso regression analysis of the single neuron model results.

claim: Scale factors for leak and sodium conductance, axoplasm resistance, and tight junction resistance also controlled CV changes during demyelination.
source: Scale factors for leak and sodium conductance, axoplasm resistance, and tight junction resistance also controlled CV changes during demyelination.
evidence: This is a finding from the Lasso regression analysis of the single neuron model results.

claim: The CV recovered more as both the remyelination and the lamellae restoration percentages increased.
source: The CV recovered more as both the remyelination and the lamellae restoration percentages increased.
evidence: This is a finding from the single neuron model simulations of remyelination.

claim: When all demyelinated segments were subsequently remyelinated with sufficient lamellae – and none of the perturbed segments were bare – the CV recovered substantially and almost no AP failed.
source: When all demyelinated segments were subsequently remyelinated with sufficient lamellae – and none of the perturbed segments were bare – the CV recovered substantially and almost no AP failed (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is a finding from the single neuron model simulations, supported by Figure 4B and C.

claim: When all demyelinated segments were remyelinated, there was a positive relationship between the initial demyelination rate and the CV recovery: CV recovered more when 75% of the segments were demyelinated than when only 25% were affected.
source: When all demyelinated segments were remyelinated, there was a positive relationship between the initial demyelination rate and the CV recovery: CV recovered more when 75% of the segments were demyelinated (Figure 4B, black lines) than when only 25% were affected.
evidence: This is a finding from the single neuron model simulations, supported by Figure 4B.

claim: Axons with more transitions between long (unperturbed) and short (remyelinated) segments had slower CV.
source: This finding is consistent with observations of Scurfield and Latimer, 2018, in which axons with more transitions between long (unperturbed) and short (remyelinated) segments had slower CV (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the single neuron model simulations, consistent with a cited study and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: When incomplete remyelination left some segments bare, there was a negative relationship between the initial amount of demyelination and CV recovery: axons with more bare segments had reduced electrical insulation, and therefore recovered less.
source: When incomplete remyelination left some segments bare (Figure 4B, colored lines), there was a negative relationship between the initial amount of demyelination and CV recovery: axons with more bare segments had reduced electrical insulation, and therefore recovered less.
evidence: This is a finding from the single neuron model simulations with an inference about the mechanism, supported by Figure 4B.

claim: Remyelinating all previously demyelinated segments, even adding just 10% of lamellae, brought AP failure rates down to 14.6±5.1%.
source: Remyelinating all previously demyelinated segments, even adding just 10% of lamellae, brought AP failure rates down to 14.6±5.1%.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the single neuron model simulations.

claim: Remyelinating all affected segments with 75% of lamellae (the maximal amount of remyelination) nearly eliminated AP failures (1.8±1.1%).
source: Remyelinating all affected segments with 75% of lamellae (the maximal amount of remyelination) nearly eliminated AP failures (1.8±1.1%).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the single neuron model simulations.

claim: When one eighth of segments were remyelinated with the maximal amount of lamellae and one eighth were left bare, 25.7±11.5% of APs failed across the cohort.
source: For example, when one eighth of segments were remyelinated with the maximal amount of lamellae and one eighth were left bare, 25.7±11.5% of APs failed across the cohort (Figure 4C, red dashed line and arrow).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the single neuron model simulations, supported by Figure 4C.

claim: AP failure rates were slightly lower when starting with partial demyelination: 10.6±7.6% of APs failed in the analogous paradigm.
source: AP failure rates were slightly lower when starting with partial demyelination: 10.6±7.6% of APs failed in the analogous paradigm (Figure 4F, red dashed line and arrow).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the single neuron model simulations, supported by Figure 4F.

claim: Combinations of demyelinated and remyelinated segments often led to sizable CV delays and AP failures.
source: In short, combinations of demyelinated and remyelinated segments often led to sizable CV delays and AP failures.
evidence: This is a summary finding from the single neuron model simulations.

claim: Propagation delays, even larger than those quantified with the single neuron model, had no effect on the network performance.
source: We found that propagation delays, even larger than those quantified with the single neuron model, had no effect on the network performance.
evidence: This is a finding from the network model simulations.

claim: Only unrealistically long delays led to a slight decrease in performance.
source: Only unrealistically long delays led to a slight decrease in performance (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the network model simulations, supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The network operates in an asynchronous state with irregular neural activity in which the timing of individual spikes does not affect network function.
source: This was as expected because, by design, the network operates in an asynchronous state with irregular neural activity in which the timing of individual spikes does not affect network function.
evidence: This is an explanation based on the design of the network model.

claim: AP failures had a large impact on network performance.
source: AP failures, on the other hand, did have a large impact.
evidence: This is a finding from the network model simulations.

claim: For AP failure probabilities matched to the distribution of AP failure probabilities across the cohort of 50 single neurons, a decay of the activity bump (i.e. reduced memory strength over time) was observed in the network model.
source: For AP failure probabilities matched to the distribution of AP failure probabilities across the cohort of 50 single neurons above, we observed a decay of the activity bump (i.e. reduced memory strength over time) in the network model.
evidence: This is a finding from the network model simulations.

claim: Decay of the activity bump can ultimately lead to extinction of the activity bump during the delay period, representing complete forgetting of the remembered stimulus (reduced memory duration).
source: This can ultimately lead to extinction of the activity bump during the delay period, representing complete forgetting of the remembered stimulus (reduced memory duration; Figure 5B, ii and iii, Figure 5C, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from the network model simulations, supported by multiple figures.

claim: For a mild reduction of the bump amplitude, memory duration was not affected but memory diffusion increased compared to the control network.
source: For a mild reduction of the bump amplitude, memory duration was not affected (Figure 5C, purple line) but memory diffusion increased compared to the control network (Figure 5B, iii and Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a finding from the network model simulations, supported by multiple figures.

claim: The bump diffusion depends inversely on the squared bump amplitude.
source: This increase in memory diffusion is consistent with mathematical analysis of firing rate models showing that the bump diffusion depends inversely on the squared bump amplitude (Kilpatrick and Ermentrout, 2013; Esnaola-Acebes et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to mathematical analyses.

claim: The memory duration was not affected when removing up to 55% of myelin lamellae per myelinated segment, regardless of the percentage of axonal segments that were altered along an axon.
source: We found that the memory duration was not affected when removing up to 55% of myelin lamellae per myelinated segment, regardless of the percentage of axonal segments that were altered along an axon (Figure 6A, left panel).
evidence: This is a finding from the network model simulations, supported by Figure 6A.

claim: When between 55% and 75% of the myelin lamellae were removed, the memory duration began to decrease, depending on the percentage of axonal segments that were demyelinated.
source: However, when between 55% and 75% of the myelin lamellae were removed, the memory duration began to decrease, depending on the percentage of axonal segments that were demyelinated.
evidence: This is a finding from the network model simulations.

claim: Increasing the percentage of demyelinated segments from 10% to 50% led to a progressive impairment, whereas an increase to 75% of the segments did not impair memory duration further.
source: In this case, increasing the percentage of demyelinated segments from 10% to 50% led to a progressive impairment, whereas an increase to 75% of the segments did not impair memory duration further.
evidence: This is a finding from the network model simulations.

claim: In cases where 100% of the myelin lamellae were removed, the memory duration dropped to ≤1 s, regardless of the percentage of segments that were demyelinated.
source: Finally, in cases where 100% of the myelin lamellae were removed, the memory duration dropped to ≤1 s, regardless of the percentage of segments that were demyelinated.
evidence: This is a finding from the network model simulations.

claim: Memory diffusion increased, i.e., working memory became less precise starting when removing between 25% and 50% of the myelin lamellae.
source: In a similar trend, memory diffusion increased, i.e., working memory became less precise starting when removing between 25% and 50% of the myelin lamellae (Figure 6B, left panel).
evidence: This is a finding from the network model simulations, supported by Figure 6B.

claim: There was a progressive impairment in memory diffusion, depending on the percentage of myelin lamellae removed and the percentage of myelinated segments affected, with a ceiling effect when more than 50% of segments were demyelinated.
source: Again, we found a progressive impairment, depending on the percentage of myelin lamellae removed and the percentage of myelinated segments affected, with a ceiling effect when more than 50% of segments were demyelinated.
evidence: This is a finding from the network model simulations.

claim: Remyelination of all previously demyelinated segments (100%), independently of the degree of demyelination, recovered the memory duration to the control networks-like performance.
source: We observed that remyelination of all previously demyelinated segments (100%), independently of the degree of demyelination, recovered the memory duration to the control networks-like performance (Figure 6A, middle and right panels; black lines).
evidence: This is a finding from the network model simulations, supported by Figure 6A.

claim: Working memory precision is not fully recovered in all cases of complete remyelination, indicated by an increase in the diffusion constant.
source: However, working memory precision is not fully recovered in all these cases, indicated by an increase in the diffusion constant (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a finding from the network model simulations, supported by Figure 6B.

claim: The performance of control networks was completely recovered only when 75% of the myelin lamellae were added back to the remyelinated segments.
source: The performance of control networks was completely recovered only when 75% of the myelin lamellae were added back to the remyelinated segments.
evidence: This is a finding from the network model simulations.

claim: Despite the new shorter and thinner myelin sheaths compared to the original intact ones, complete remyelination is able to recover control, unperturbed network function.
source: Thus, despite the new shorter and thinner myelin sheaths compared to the original intact ones, complete remyelination is able to recover control, unperturbed network function.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the network model simulations.

claim: Memory diffusion was partly recovered compared to the complete demyelination case when 50–75% of the demyelinated segments were remyelinated, but it remained far from the performance of the control network.
source: Memory diffusion was partly recovered compared to the complete demyelination case (compare left and middle panels in Figure 6B) when 50–75% of the demyelinated segments were remyelinated, but it remained far from the performance of the control network.
evidence: This is a finding from the network model simulations, supported by Figure 6B.

claim: Incomplete remyelination was unable to restore network function when bare axon (completely demyelinated) segments were present.
source: In sum, incomplete remyelination was unable to restore network function when bare axon (completely demyelinated) segments were present.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the network model simulations.

claim: When 25% to 75% of the previously only partially demyelinated segments were remyelinated, both memory duration and memory diffusion were restored closer to the values of the control networks.
source: However, when we remyelinated between 25% and 75% of the previously only partially demyelinated segments, both memory duration and memory diffusion were restored closer to the values of the control networks (Figure 6A and B, right panel).
evidence: This is a finding from the network model simulations, supported by Figure 6A and B.

claim: AP failures corresponding to demyelination caused working memory errors qualitatively similar to the delay-active network in an activity-silent model.
source: We found that AP failures corresponding to demyelination caused working memory errors qualitatively similar to the delay-active network (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the activity-silent network model simulations, supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: Increasing propagation delays did not lead to additional working memory errors in the activity-silent model, unless unrealistically high values were included.
source: On the other hand, increasing propagation delays did not lead to additional working memory errors, unless we include unrealistically high values (uniform distribution in the range of 0–100 ms; Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the activity-silent network model simulations, supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: The main findings do not critically depend on the exact working memory mechanism (active vs. activity-silent).
source: These results are qualitatively similar to the delay-active network model. Thus, our main findings do not critically depend on the exact working memory mechanism (active vs. activity-silent).
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing the delay-active and activity-silent network models.

claim: The performance was impaired – memory duration significantly decreased and memory diffusion significantly increased – when the percentage of normal sheaths decreased.
source: We observed that the performance was impaired – memory duration significantly decreased (Figure 7B), and memory diffusion significantly increased (Figure 7C) – when the percentage of normal sheaths decreased.
evidence: This is a finding from the network model simulations with heterogeneous myelin alterations, supported by Figure 7B and C.

claim: These results are consistent with an experimentally observed increased cognitive impairment in various learning and working memory tasks with an age-related decrease of the percentage of normal sheaths in dlPFC of rhesus monkeys.
source: These results are consistent with an experimentally observed increased cognitive impairment in various learning and working memory tasks (including the delayed recognition span task, a spatial working memory task) with an age-related decrease of the percentage of normal sheaths in dlPFC of rhesus monkeys (Peters and Sethares, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to an empirical study and consistency with the model results.

claim: Myelin alterations alone can account for significant working memory impairment, pointing to demyelination as a key factor in age-related working memory decline.
source: Importantly, our results indicate that myelin alterations alone can account for significant working memory impairment, pointing to demyelination as a key factor in age-related working memory decline.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the network model simulations with heterogeneous myelin alterations.

claim: Empirical studies have found an age-dependent increase in the percentage of paranodal profiles, indicative of more and shorter myelin sheaths, from 5% in young monkeys to 17% in aged monkeys.
source: Empirical studies have found an age-dependent increase in the percentage of paranodal profiles, indicative of more and shorter myelin sheaths, from 5% in young monkeys to 17% in aged monkeys (Peters and Sethares, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to an empirical study.

claim: Performance was significantly impaired compared to the young, control networks with intact myelin when simulating networks with up to 45% of new myelin sheaths: memory duration decreased to almost 1 s and diffusion constant increased.
source: We simulated networks with up to a 45% of new myelin sheaths and we observed that performance was significantly impaired compared to the young, control networks with intact myelin: memory duration decreased to almost 1 s (Figure 8B) and diffusion constant increased (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is a finding from the network model simulations with remyelination, supported by Figure 8B and C.

claim: This is consistent with empirical findings showing that cognitive impairment for a cohort of 18 young and aged rhesus monkeys increased with an increase of the percentage of paranodal profiles in the dlPFC.
source: This is consistent with empirical findings showing that cognitive impairment for a cohort of 18 young and aged rhesus monkeys increased with an increase of the percentage of paranodal profiles in the dlPFC (Peters and Sethares, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to an empirical study and consistency with the model results.

claim: Both demyelination and incomplete remyelination lead to impaired performance in the networks, compared to networks with intact myelin sheaths.
source: Therefore, both demyelination and incomplete remyelination lead to impaired performance in our networks, compared to networks with intact myelin sheaths.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the network model simulations.

claim: The novelty of the neuron model lies in its systematic exploration of a combination of different myelin perturbation types known to occur in myelin dystrophies, across a wide range of biologically feasible models.
source: The novelty of our neuron model lies in its systematic exploration of a combination of different myelin perturbation types known to occur in myelin dystrophies, across a wide range of biologically feasible models.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the study's approach.

claim: The single neuron model assumed that age-related myelin dystrophies alter the insulative properties of lamellae analogously to demyelination.
source: Our single neuron model assumed that age-related myelin dystrophies (e.g. Figure 1) alter the insulative properties of lamellae analogously to demyelination, and examined interactions between demyelination and remyelination.
evidence: This is a statement about the assumptions of the single neuron model.

claim: Past studies of myelin dystrophy examined how either demyelination or remyelination of all segments affected AP propagation for a few representative axon morphologies.
source: Past studies of myelin dystrophy examined how either demyelination or remyelination of all segments affected AP propagation for a few representative axon morphologies.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of past studies.

claim: Scurfield and Latimer, 2018, explored how remyelination affected CV delays, finding that axons with more transitions between long and short myelinated segments had slower CV.
source: For example, Scurfield and Latimer, 2018, explored how remyelination affected CV delays, finding that axons with more transitions between long and short myelinated segments had slower CV (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), and was first to explore how remyelination interacts with tight junctions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study and reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Scurfield and Latimer, 2018, was first to explore how remyelination interacts with tight junctions.
source: For example, Scurfield and Latimer, 2018, explored how remyelination affected CV delays, finding that axons with more transitions between long and short myelinated segments had slower CV (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), and was first to explore how remyelination interacts with tight junctions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Scurfield and Latimer, 2018, did not couple remyelination and demyelination together or examine AP failures.
source: However, their study did not couple remyelination and demyelination together or examine AP failures.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of a previous study.

claim: Demyelination caused CV slowing and eventual AP failures.
source: Other basic findings from our single neuron cohort are consistent with past modeling studies, including that demyelination caused CV slowing and eventual AP failures (Stephanova et al., 2005; Stephanova and Daskalova, 2008; Naud and Longtin, 2019), and, separately, that remyelination with shorter and thinner myelinated segments led to CV slowing (Lasiene et al., 2008; Powers et al., 2012; Scurfield and Latimer, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to past modeling studies and consistency with the current study's findings.

claim: Remyelination with shorter and thinner myelinated segments led to CV slowing.
source: Other basic findings from our single neuron cohort are consistent with past modeling studies, including that demyelination caused CV slowing and eventual AP failures (Stephanova et al., 2005; Stephanova and Daskalova, 2008; Naud and Longtin, 2019), and, separately, that remyelination with shorter and thinner myelinated segments led to CV slowing (Lasiene et al., 2008; Powers et al., 2012; Scurfield and Latimer, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to past modeling studies and consistency with the current study's findings.

claim: By assuming that some previously demyelinated segments were remyelinated while others were not, models could have much higher AP failure rates than previously reported.
source: However, by assuming that some previously demyelinated segments were remyelinated while others were not, we found that models could have much higher AP failure rates than previously reported.
evidence: This is a finding from the single neuron model simulations that differs from previous studies.

claim: A few neurons in the cohort showed a CV increase after remyelination, which has not generally been reported before and is likely due to an interplay between ion channels in the new nodes and altered electrotonic lengths in the perturbed myelinated segments.
source: We also found a few neurons in our cohort showing a CV increase after remyelination, which has not generally been reported before and is likely due to an interplay between ion channels in the new nodes and altered electrotonic lengths in the perturbed myelinated segments (e.g. Moore et al., 1978; Naud and Longtin, 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from the single neuron model simulations with a speculative explanation supported by citations.

claim: Parameters including axon diameter, node length, length of myelinated segments, and nodal ion channel densities predicted how the models responded to demyelination and remyelination.
source: Parameters including axon diameter, node length, length of myelinated segments, and nodal ion channel densities predicted how our models responded to demyelination and remyelination; these findings are consistent with past modeling studies over more limited parameter ranges (e.g. Goldman and Albus, 1968; Moore et al., 1978; Babbs and Shi, 2013; Young et al., 2013; Schmidt and Knösche, 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from the Lasso regression analysis, consistent with past modeling studies.

claim: Better empirical measurements of axon parameters in monkey dlPFC would help predict the extent to which myelin dystrophy and remyelination along individual axons with aging affect AP propagation.
source: Better empirical measurements of these parameters in monkey dlPFC, e.g., from three-dimensional electron microscopy studies or single neuron axon studies combined with markers for myelin, would help predict the extent to which myelin dystrophy and remyelination along individual axons with aging affect AP propagation.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future empirical work based on the model findings.

claim: The multicompartment model was constrained by morphological and physiological data in rhesus monkey dlPFC.
source: Another important feature of our multicompartment model is that it was constrained by morphological and physiological data in rhesus monkey dlPFC –an extremely valuable dataset from an animal model with many similarities to humans (Upright and Baxter, 2021; Tarantal et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a statement about the model's constraints, supported by citations.

claim: The computational infrastructure enables simultaneous investigations of signal propagation through the dendritic arbor and axon.
source: While beyond the scope of the current study, this computational infrastructure – with a detailed axon, initial segment, soma, and apical and basal dendrites – enables simultaneous investigations of signal propagation through the dendritic arbor and axon.
evidence: This is a statement about the capabilities of the model for future studies.

claim: The model can be extended to explore interactions between spatially localized myelin perturbations and axon collateralization.
source: Our model can also be extended to explore interactions between spatially localized myelin perturbations (such as those seen in multiple sclerosis) and axon collateralization (Sengupta et al., 2023), which would affect the distance dependence of AP failures.
evidence: This is a statement about potential extensions of the model, supported by citation.

claim: Integrating results from single neuron models into network models of working memory is a powerful way to connect empirical data across multiple scales.
source: Integrating such results from single neuron models into network models of working memory, as we have done here, is a powerful way to connect empirical data across multiple scales.
evidence: This is a statement about the value of the multiscale modeling approach.

claim: Increasing probabilities of AP failure, corresponding to higher degrees of demyelination, gradually impaired working memory precision and the time during which stimulus information can be held in memory.
source: With the spiking neural network model, we found that increasing probabilities of AP failure, corresponding to higher degrees of demyelination, gradually impaired working memory precision and the time during which stimulus information can be held in memory.
evidence: This is a finding from the network model simulations.

claim: Complete remyelination of all previously demyelinated segments restored performance to the control network level.
source: Complete remyelination of all previously demyelinated segments restored performance to the control network level.
evidence: This is a finding from the network model simulations.

claim: Introducing propagation delays to mimic AP slowing, in the time range of the delays quantified with the single neuron model, did not have an effect on network performance.
source: In contrast to the strong impact of AP failures on network function, introducing propagation delays to mimic AP slowing, in the time range of the delays quantified with the single neuron model, did not have an effect (Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the network model simulations, supported by figures.

claim: The network operates in an asynchronous state in which the dynamics are primarily governed by the statistics of neuronal activity (e.g. firing rates), rather than precise spike timings.
source: This is because the network operates in an asynchronous state in which the dynamics are primarily governed by the statistics of neuronal activity (e.g. firing rates), rather than precise spike timings (van Vreeswijk and Sompolinsky, 1996; Hansel and Mato, 2013).
evidence: This is an explanation for why propagation delays had no effect, supported by citations.

claim: Highly irregular persistent activity is observed in PFC during working memory tasks.
source: While highly irregular persistent activity is indeed observed in PFC during working memory tasks (Compte et al., 2003), at the mesoscopic level oscillations of the local field potentials and synchronization also play an important role (Gregoriou et al., 2009; Liebe et al., 2012; Buschman et al., 2012; Salazar et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: At the mesoscopic level oscillations of the local field potentials and synchronization play an important role in PFC during working memory tasks.
source: While highly irregular persistent activity is indeed observed in PFC during working memory tasks (Compte et al., 2003), at the mesoscopic level oscillations of the local field potentials and synchronization also play an important role (Gregoriou et al., 2009; Liebe et al., 2012; Buschman et al., 2012; Salazar et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: AP slowing may alter neural oscillations and synchrony which could lead to further working memory impairment not captured by the network model.
source: AP slowing may alter these neural oscillations and synchrony which could lead to further working memory impairment not captured by our network model.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential effects not captured by the current model.

claim: The network model predicts an age-related increase in systematic errors (bias) due to an increased drift of the activity bump.
source: In addition to age-related changes in memory duration and precision, our network model predicts an age-related increase in systematic errors (bias) due to an increased drift of the activity bump (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a prediction from the network model, supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: If demyelination is spatially localized in a part of the network, the model predicts a repulsive bias away from the memories encoded in the affected zone.
source: Moreover, if demyelination is spatially localized in a part of the network, the model predicts a repulsive bias away from the memories encoded in the affected zone (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a prediction from the network model, supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Delay-dependent systematic working memory errors have been observed in behavioral experiments.
source: Delay-dependent systematic working memory errors have been observed in behavioral experiments (Panichello et al., 2019; Bae, 2021; Stein et al., 2021) and it would be interesting to test whether those biases also change with aging.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Working memory is likely sustained by interactions between several fronto-parietal brain areas.
source: In addition to the prefrontal cortex, working memory is likely sustained by interactions between several fronto-parietal brain areas (Leavitt et al., 2017; Christophel et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: For biologically realistic combinations of neurons with intact and demyelinated axons, the network model predicts that myelin dystrophies alone would lead to spatial working memory impairment with aging.
source: For biologically realistic combinations of neurons with intact and demyelinated axons, our network model predicts that myelin dystrophies alone would lead to spatial working memory impairment with aging (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a prediction from the network model, supported by Figure 7.

claim: This result supports the observation that cognitive impairment increases as the percentage of normal myelin sheaths decreases.
source: This result supports the observation that cognitive impairment increases as the percentage of normal myelin sheaths decreases (Peters and Sethares, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to an empirical study and consistency with the model results.

claim: Combining neurons containing either intact or incompletely remyelinated axons, spatial working memory is still impaired in the context of incomplete remyelination.
source: In addition, combining neurons containing either intact or incompletely remyelinated axons, we found that spatial working memory is still impaired in the context of incomplete remyelination (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a finding from the network model simulations, supported by Figure 8.

claim: The result explains the positive correlation between cognitive impairment and a higher percentage of new, shorter and thinner, myelin sheaths.
source: Our result explains two separate empirical findings. One study showed a positive correlation between cognitive impairment and a higher percentage of new, shorter and thinner, myelin sheaths (Peters and Sethares, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to an empirical study and consistency with the model results.

claim: In the single neuron model, insufficiently remyelinated axons with an array of long unperturbed, long thin, and new shorter and thinner segments had slower CV and more AP failures compared to unperturbed axons.
source: In our single neuron model, insufficiently remyelinated axons with an array of long unperturbed, long thin, and new shorter and thinner segments had slower CV and more AP failures compared to unperturbed axons.
evidence: This is a finding from the single neuron model simulations.

claim: With aging, oligodendroglia has a decreased capacity for effective maturation, remaining in a progenitor state without being able to produce new myelin.
source: A second study found that, with aging, oligodendroglia has a decreased capacity for effective maturation, remaining in a progenitor state without being able to produce new myelin.
evidence: This is a statement about an empirical finding from a second study.

claim: Low capacity for remyelination was correlated with spatial working memory impairment in monkeys.
source: This low capacity for remyelination was correlated with spatial working memory impairment in the monkeys (Dimovasili et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to an empirical study.

claim: Axons with demyelinated segments, or otherwise poorly insulated myelin sheaths, experience delayed and even failed AP propagation, which in turn led to working memory impairment.
source: Our models showed that axons with demyelinated segments, or otherwise poorly insulated myelin sheaths, experience delayed and even failed AP propagation, which in turn led to working memory impairment.
evidence: This is a finding from the computational models.

claim: It is reasonable to assume that ineffective remyelination may lead to working memory impairment.
source: Therefore, it is reasonable to assume that ineffective remyelination may lead to working memory impairment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the model findings and empirical observations.

claim: Complete remyelination of all previously demyelinated segments with sufficient myelin, with fewer transitions between long and short segments, led to full recovery of working memory function.
source: In fact, complete remyelination of all previously demyelinated segments with sufficient myelin, with fewer transitions between long and short segments, led to full recovery of working memory function.
evidence: This is a finding from the network model simulations.

claim: Differences in the degree of demyelination or remyelination may account for the cognitive variability observed across individuals with aging.
source: Our findings also suggest that differences in the degree of demyelination or remyelination (Figures 7 and 8) may account for the cognitive variability observed across individuals with aging, which encompass individuals with both good (successful agers) and impaired (unsuccessful agers) cognitive function (Lacreuse et al., 2005; Moore et al., 2006; Moss et al., 2007; Moore et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a suggestion based on the model findings, supported by citations to empirical studies and figures.

claim: The previous work modeled increased AP firing rates observed in vitro together with the loss of both excitatory and inhibitory synapses, and quantified how these alterations affected working memory performance.
source: Our previous work (Ibañez et al., 2019) modeled increased AP firing rates observed in vitro together with the loss of both excitatory and inhibitory synapses, and quantified how these alterations affected working memory performance.
evidence: This is a statement about previous work by the authors, supported by citation.

claim: Aged networks which compensated the loss of excitatory and inhibitory synapses with higher firing rates in individual pyramidal neurons successfully retained memory of the DRT stimulus.
source: Aged networks which compensated the loss of excitatory and inhibitory synapses with higher firing rates in individual pyramidal neurons successfully retained memory of the DRT stimulus.
evidence: This is a finding from previous work by the authors.

claim: Networks in which the overall excitatory drive to pyramidal neurons was also decreased reproduced the lower firing rates during performance of DRT in aged monkeys, reported in Wang et al., 2011.
source: In addition, networks in which we also decreased the overall excitatory drive to pyramidal neurons reproduced the lower firing rates during performance of DRT in aged monkeys, reported in Wang et al., 2011.
evidence: This is a finding from previous work by the authors, supported by citation to an empirical study.

claim: Decreased excitation could arise from AP failures induced by myelin dystrophy.
source: Such decreased excitation could arise from AP failures induced by myelin dystrophy, as shown here.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the current study's findings to previous work.

claim: It has been hypothesized that the hyperexcitability of dlPFC pyramidal neurons observed in vitro with aging could be a homeostatic mechanism to compensate for AP disruptions due to dystrophic myelin.
source: It has also been hypothesized that the hyperexcitability of dlPFC pyramidal neurons observed in vitro with aging could be a homeostatic mechanism to compensate for AP disruptions due to dystrophic myelin (Luebke et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: The multicompartment model used here is particularly well suited to simultaneous modeling of alterations in the soma, dendrites, synapses, and axon of individual pyramidal neurons.
source: The multicompartment model used here is particularly well suited to simultaneous modeling of alterations in the soma, dendrites, synapses, and axon of individual pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This is a statement about the capabilities of the model.

claim: Myelin dystrophy occurs in many neurological conditions, including multiple sclerosis, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, autism spectrum disorders, and after traumatic brain injury.
source: Myelin dystrophy occurs in many neurological conditions, including multiple sclerosis, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, autism spectrum disorders, and after traumatic brain injury (Franklin and Ffrench-Constant, 2008; Takahashi et al., 2011; Armstrong et al., 2016; Gouvêa-Junqueira et al., 2020; Galvez-Contreras et al., 2020; Simkins et al., 2021; Valdés-Tovar et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies and reviews.

claim: Working memory is often one of the most vulnerable cognitive functions in conditions with myelin dystrophy, especially schizophrenia or autism spectrum disorders.
source: As in normal aging working memory is often one of the most vulnerable cognitive functions in these conditions, especially schizophrenia or autism spectrum disorders (Wang et al., 2017; Hahn et al., 2018; Gold and Luck, 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Myelin changes alone can account for working memory impairment.
source: Since we found that myelin changes alone can account for working memory impairment, our study points to myelin degradation as a key factor in working memory decline with normal aging and, perhaps, in neuropathological conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the computational models.

claim: The study points to myelin degradation as a key factor in working memory decline with normal aging and, perhaps, in neuropathological conditions.
source: Since we found that myelin changes alone can account for working memory impairment, our study points to myelin degradation as a key factor in working memory decline with normal aging and, perhaps, in neuropathological conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the computational models with speculation about broader implications.

claim: The g-ratio among models in the cohort was 0.71±0.02, with total axon lengths of 1.2±0.1 cm.
source: The g-ratio (ratio of axon to fiber diameter) among models in the cohort was 0.71±0.02, with total axon lengths of 1.2±0.1 cm.
evidence: This is a quantitative description of the model cohort.

claim: Neuropil from a 10-year-old monkey shows healthy and compact myelin visible as thick outlines surrounding nerve fibers which have been sectioned at their internodes.
source: Neuropil from a 10-year-old monkey. Healthy and compact myelin is visible as thick outlines surrounding nerve fibers which have been sectioned at their internodes.
evidence: This is a description of Figure 1A showing empirical data.

claim: Neuropil from a 27-year-old monkey shows dystrophic myelin surrounding nerve fibers, presenting a splitting of the major dense line of the myelin sheaths and balloons.
source: Neuropil from a 27-year-old monkey. Arrows indicate dystrophic myelin surrounding nerve fibers, presenting a splitting of the major dense line of the myelin sheaths (left and right arrows) and balloons (left and middle arrows).
evidence: This is a description of Figure 1B showing empirical data.
